title: An exponential query advantage from access to Stinespring dilation unitaries in quantum channel learning
authors: Manaki Arihara, Satoshi Yoshida, Philip Taranto, Mio Murao
abstract: We present a learning task for quantum channels that exhibits an exponential separation in query complexity (in terms of the number of qubits) between two access models: i) black-box channel access and ii) access to a Stinespring dilation unitary of the channel along with its inverse. We consider the task of learning how close the unknown channel is to the set of unitary channels. This is characterized by the \textit{optimal average gate fidelity (OAGF)}, defined as the average gate fidelity maximized over all unitary channels. For constant Kraus rank and a dilation environment of dimension $\operatorname{polylog}(d)$, we provide an algorithm that estimates the OAGF to fixed additive accuracy using $\operatorname{polylog}(d)$ queries to the Stinespring dilation unitary and its inverse. In contradistinction, under the black-box access model, this estimation requires at least $Ω(\sqrt{d})$ queries, even for channels of constant Kraus rank and constant additive accuracy. As a corollary, we rule out a universal simulator that uses only $\operatorname{poly}(\log d,q)$ queries to the unknown channel to approximate the output of arbitrary $q$-query algorithms with access to a randomly-sampled Stinespring dilation unitary and its inverse, even to sufficiently small constant error. These results demonstrate that access to the system-environment joint evolution and its inverse can provide an exponential advantage in estimating an intrinsic property of a quantum channel.
summary: This paper proves an exponential separation in query complexity for estimating the Optimal Average Gate Fidelity (OAGF) of a quantum channel. By comparing black-box access to the channel versus access to its Stinespring dilation unitary, the authors show that the former requires $\Omega(\sqrt{d})$ queries, while the latter requires only polynomially many queries. This highlights the immense computational advantage gained by understanding the underlying system-environment coupling.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate an exponential separation in query complexity for estimating an intrinsic property of a quantum channel (the Optimal Average Gate Fidelity, OAGF) depending on the access model.
main_result: Access to the Stinespring dilation unitary and its inverse allows for the estimation of OAGF with polynomially many queries, whereas black-box access requires $\Omega(\sqrt{d})$ queries, establishing an exponential separation.
method: The analysis uses quantum information theory tools, including Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) and lower-bound arguments based on distinguishing quantum ensembles, to compare query complexity.
model_or_system: The study concerns quantum channels $E: \mathcal{L}(H) 	o \mathcal{L}(H)$ acting on a $d$-dimensional system Hilbert space $H$. The comparison is between direct black-box access to $E$ and access to its Stinespring dilation unitary $U_m$ and its inverse.
key_observables: Optimal Average Gate Fidelity (OAGF) and Optimal Entanglement Fidelity (OEF).
important_parameters: System dimension $d$, Kraus rank $r$ (assumed constant), and the required additive accuracy $\epsilon$.
main_assumptions: The separation holds for constant Kraus rank and polynomially bounded environment dimensions. The lower bound relies on the existence of a universal simulator.
figures_summary: Figure 3 details the state evolution using path-recording oracles $P$ and $P^\#$ to analyze the difference between states derived from the dilation unitary access.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by defining the OAGF and comparing two access models. It derives an upper bound using the dilation unitary (via QSVT) and then establishes a lower bound using channel discrimination arguments, culminating in the proof of the exponential separation.
why_interesting: This work provides a fundamental resource-theoretic result showing that knowing the system-environment joint evolution (the unitary) provides exponentially more computational power for quantum process characterization than simply querying the channel output directly.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Original t-query algorithm with Haar-random unitary channels. The unitary channels V and U are independently chosen from the Haar measure and the same unitary channels are used in every query to the composite oracle U ◦Wb ◦V. The quantum operations A0, . . . , At are arbitrary operations independent of the oracles U, Wb and V, and represent the intermediate processing of the algorithm on the target system S and the ancilla system S′. Each invocation of Wb produces an environment register Ei, which is traced out at the end. Averaging the resulting output state over U and V gives ρb(t).

Figure 2: First hybrid in the path-recording argument. Every Haar-random unitary channel V in Fig. 1 is replaced by the restricted path-recording oracle P#, while U remains Haar-random. The oracle P# acts jointly on the target system S and the relation register R1, recording the relation xi 7→(αi, ui) generated at the i-th query. The operations A0, . . . , At, the channel Wb, and the environment registers Ei are not changed from the original algorithm. After tracing out R1 and the environment system and averaging over the remaining Haar-random unitary U, the circuit yields the first hybrid state ρ(1) b (t).

Figure 3: Second hybrid in the path-recording argument. In addition to replacing V by the restricted path-recording oracle P#, every Haar-random unitary channel U is replaced by the standard path- recording oracle P. At the i-th query, P# records the transition xi 7→(αi, ui) in the relation register R1, Wb produces the corresponding environment state |wb,αi⟩Ei, and P records the subsequent transition (αi, ui) 7→zi in the relation register R2. Thus, after t queries, R1 and R2 store the relations R1(⃗x, ⃗α, ⃗u) and R2(⃗α, ⃗u, ⃗z), respectively. Tracing out the two relation registers and the environment system yields the second hybrid state ρ(2) b (t).
